facts.claim: The raid on Lindisfarne opened the Viking Age in Britain
facts.context: Norse raiders sacked the monastery on Lindisfarne in 793, shocking Christian Europe.
facts.goDeeper: Monasteries were targets because they were rich, coastal and undefended.

facts.claim: Norse sailors established a settlement in North America
facts.context: Tree-ring dating of wood at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland gives an exact year of 1021.
facts.goDeeper: That is 471 years before Columbus, and it is the only confirmed Norse site in the Americas.

facts.claim: The Viking Age is usually said to end with the Norman Conquest
facts.context: 1066 saw both the defeat of Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge and William's victory at Hastings.
facts.goDeeper: William's Normans were themselves descended from Norse settlers in France.

facts.claim: Norse settlers began colonising Iceland
facts.context: Traditional settlement date is around 874, when Ingolfr Arnarson founded Reykjavik.
facts.goDeeper: Iceland's parliament, the Althing, was founded in 930 and is among the oldest still sitting.

facts.claim: Erik the Red led settlers to Greenland
facts.context: Erik, exiled from Iceland, established Norse colonies in Greenland around 985.
facts.goDeeper: He called it Greenland to attract settlers, which may be the earliest recorded property marketing.

facts.claim: The Great Heathen Army landed in England
facts.context: A large Norse force arrived in East Anglia in 865, intent on conquest rather than raiding.
facts.goDeeper: Within a decade it had destroyed three of the four English kingdoms. Only Wessex held.

facts.claim: Top speed of a Viking longship under sail
facts.context: Reconstructions have reached about 15 knots, quick even by later standards.
facts.goDeeper: The shallow draught mattered more than the speed: a longship could sail up a river and land on a beach.

facts.claim: Typical crew of a large Viking longship
facts.context: Larger warships carried perhaps 60 to 70 men, with oars for when the wind failed.
facts.goDeeper: The biggest recorded ships were far larger, but most raids used vessels of this size.

facts.claim: Alfred the Great and Guthrum agreed the treaty creating the Danelaw
facts.context: After Alfred's victory at Edington, a treaty divided England, leaving the north and east under Danish law.
facts.goDeeper: Hundreds of English place names ending in -by and -thorpe are still Norse.

facts.claim: The Norse leader Rollo was granted the land that became Normandy
facts.context: The Frankish king ceded territory around Rouen to Rollo in 911 to stop the raiding.
facts.goDeeper: 'Normandy' simply means the land of the Northmen.

facts.claim: The Oseberg ship burial was excavated in Norway
facts.context: A remarkably preserved ninth-century ship containing the burial of two women.
facts.goDeeper: Who they were is still unknown; the richness of the grave suggests very high status.

facts.claim: The Varangian Guard was formed from Norse warriors in Constantinople
facts.context: The Byzantine emperor Basil II formed an elite guard of Norse and Rus fighters around 988.
facts.goDeeper: Norse traders had reached Byzantium down the rivers of Russia; some carved graffiti into the Hagia Sophia.

facts.claim: Norse forces captured York, which they called Jorvik
facts.context: Taken in 866, York became the capital of a Norse kingdom lasting almost a century.
facts.goDeeper: Excavations at Coppergate found timber houses, workshops and even preserved leather boots.

facts.claim: Vikings wore horned helmets into battle
facts.context: No horned helmet has ever been found in a Viking grave. The image comes from a 19th-century costume designer for Wagner's operas.
facts.goDeeper: Horns on a helmet would be a gift to an opponent in a fight.

facts.claim: Norse sailors reached North America before Columbus
facts.context: Confirmed by the excavated settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows, precisely dated to 1021.
facts.goDeeper: They did not stay. The sagas describe conflict with people already living there.

facts.claim: Most Norse people were farmers rather than raiders
facts.context: Raiding was seasonal work for a minority. The great majority farmed, fished and traded.
facts.goDeeper: 'Viking' was originally something you did, not something you were.

facts.claim: Norse women could own property and seek divorce
facts.context: Norse law allowed women to own land, inherit and initiate divorce — unusual in early medieval Europe.
facts.goDeeper: A woman buried at Birka with weapons and gaming pieces was confirmed by DNA in 2017 to be female.

facts.claim: The Norse had a written alphabet of their own
facts.context: The runic alphabet, or futhark, was carved into stone, wood and bone across Scandinavia.
facts.goDeeper: Thousands of runestones survive in Sweden alone, many raised as memorials rather than records.

facts.claim: Four English weekday names come from Norse gods
facts.context: Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday derive from Tyr, Odin (Woden), Thor and Frigg.
facts.goDeeper: The Norse influence on English runs deeper than vocabulary: 'they', 'them' and 'their' are Norse too.

source.title: Names of the days of the week

facts.claim: Norse men were noted by contemporaries for grooming and bathing
facts.context: English writers complained that Danish settlers combed their hair and bathed weekly, making them too attractive to local women.
facts.goDeeper: Combs are among the most common objects found on Viking-age sites.
